title: FPIs Turn Net Sellers, Pull ₹35,860 Crore From Indian Equities in September
excerpt: A two-month buying streak ended as elevated US bond yields, high crude prices and a rotation into AI-led markets pushed foreign investors to the exits, putting 2026 on track for record annual outflows.
body:
• Foreign portfolio investors withdrew ₹35,860 crore (about $4 billion) from Indian equities in September, ending a two-month buying streak.
  • Total 2026 outflows now stand near ₹2.7 lakh crore, already well above the ₹1.66 lakh crore withdrawn in all of 2025.
  • The Nifty 50 fell 6.1% and the BSE Sensex 5.8% in September, their second consecutive monthly decline.
  • The selling has carried into October: FPIs pulled ₹9,232 crore on October 1 alone, according to CDSL data.

Foreign capital walks out after two months of buying

Foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) pulled ₹35,860 crore from Indian equities in September, turning net sellers after two months of buying, as elevated US bond yields, high crude oil prices and a stronger dollar drained the appeal of Indian assets. The selling came after FPIs had invested ₹20,200 crore in July and ₹29,630 crore in August, according to NSDL data reported by The Hindu.

The September reversal took total foreign withdrawals from Indian equities in 2026 to about ₹2.7 lakh crore, already far exceeding the ₹1.66 lakh crore pulled out in all of 2025 and putting foreign investors on track for a record year of selling.

Context & Background

The exits came during a bruising month for Indian stocks. The Nifty 50 fell 6.1% and the BSE Sensex declined 5.8% in September, with both benchmarks recording their second straight monthly decline, according to Reuters. Global markets faced renewed pressure from higher interest rates, rising crude prices, geopolitical tensions and a stronger US dollar.

India's particular vulnerability is oil. As a major crude importer, higher Brent prices widen the current-account deficit, raise inflation risks and increase pressure on the rupee, while squeezing corporate margins in fuel-intensive industries. "Oil and geopolitics remain the major risk," Dheeraj Gaur, chief investment strategy officer at Choice Wealth, told The Economic Times. "Elevated crude prices are particularly a challenge for India because of their immediate impact on the current account, inflation expectations and the rupee."

Profit-booking after a strong run and rotation toward AI-led North Asian markets such as South Korea and Taiwan also drew capital away. Rajesh Singla, fund manager and CEO of Alpha AMC, told The Hindu the September selling was "largely due to factors such as elevated crude prices amid Hormuz-related supply risks, a weak rupee, firm US bond yields, profit-booking and rotation towards AI-led North Asian markets."

Impact & Analysis

Higher US Treasury yields are doing the most structural damage to the FPI bid. Rising yields raise the risk-free return available to investors and increase the opportunity cost of holding riskier emerging-market equities. Gautam Duggad, head of institutional equities sales at Motilal Oswal Financial Services, said rising US bond yields, a stronger dollar and shifting expectations around global interest rates had reduced the relative attractiveness of emerging-market equities.

NSE managing director and CEO Ashish Chauhan framed the exits as cyclical rotation rather than a verdict on India. "FPIs are fund managers who take out their money and go there for a cycle, and they do this often," he said last week, noting the AI-led rally had lifted the US market "from $25 trillion to about $75 trillion," with similar moves in Korea and Taiwan. He added that when the current AI cycle fades, some of that capital could return to India, while stressing this was his personal view.

Not every sector bled. NSDL's fortnightly data showed healthcare drew ₹2,114 crore of FPI buying in the first half of September, its sixth consecutive fortnight of inflows, as investors favored businesses with visible earnings. Financial services, automobiles, oil and gas, and FMCG bore the heaviest selling.

"FPIs are fund managers who take out their money and go there for a cycle, and they do this often."

— Ashish Chauhan, MD & CEO, NSE

What's Next

The selling has continued into October. FPIs withdrew ₹9,232 crore from Indian equities on October 1 alone, according to Central Depository Services Ltd data — suggesting the September reversal was not a month-end blip. With the US Federal Reserve signaling rates could stay higher for longer and crude elevated on Middle East tensions, the conditions that drove September's outflows remain firmly in place.

Whether October extends the streak will be an early read on whether India's record year of foreign selling continues into the December quarter. The next FPI data points — and the October rate outlook from the Fed — will set the tone for the rest of 2026.
nri_angle: For India-focused investors in the US and globally, the record pace of foreign withdrawals shows global capital is pricing Indian equities against high US yields and elevated valuations — a re-rating, not a dismissal, of the India growth story.
author: Diaspora Desk
